query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten‐based refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) that is designed with low-activation elements (i.e., avoiding elements that lead to long-lived radionuclides) will serve as a viable structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors. Its high configurational entropy is expected to improve radiation tolerance and suppress defect accumulation compared to monolithic tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline solid solution RHEA that uses tungsten as the primary matrix element combined with other refractory, low-activation alloying elements (e.g., Ta, V, or Ti) to tune properties.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simulated fusion reactor conditions, including high temperatures (≥1000 K) and dual irradiation (high flux helium implantation and neutron irradiation).
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment representative of plasma-facing components, with concurrent particle (He and neutron) bombardment and thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: The high entropy microstructure and any stepwise, coherent nanoprecipitations that form during processing, which work together to inhibit defect nucleation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: By combining tungsten with selected refractory elements to form a high-entropy alloy, the material benefits from reduced atomic diffusion and defect mobility under irradiation. The coherent interfaces (or nanoprecipitates) are anticipated to serve as effective sinks for irradiation-induced defects while the low-activation chemistry minimizes the formation of long-lived radionuclides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simulated fusion reactor conditions, the tungsten-based RHEA will generate a lower inventory of long-lived activation products, maintain superior high-temperature mechanical performance, and exhibit improved resistance to helium-induced surface degradation compared to pure tungsten used in current plasma-facing components.
generation.baseline: The currently used pure tungsten and tungsten-based alloys for plasma-facing components which show issues such as helium bubble formation and high activation under irradiation.
generation.boundary: The benefit may be contingent on achieving the proper alloy composition and microstructure; performance under varying oxygen or impurity contents and under actual reactor-scale thermal flux may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative reduction in activation levels and the exact scale of mechanical or irradiation performance improvements remain to be fully established under reactor-relevant conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the tungsten-based RHEA with the targeted low-activation composition and comparable pure tungsten reference samples. Subject both sets of samples to high-temperature (≥1000 K) testing under simultaneous helium and neutron irradiation in a fusion-relevant simulation facility. Compare the activation levels (via neutron activation analysis), surface morphology changes (using electron microscopy), and high-temperature mechanical properties (via tensile and creep tests).
measurements: Neutron activation analysis to quantify radioisotope inventories
High-resolution electron microscopy to assess defect structures and helium bubble formation
Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (tensile, creep, ductility assessments)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-based RHEA fails to exhibit statistically significant reductions in activation products and improvements in high-temperature mechanical properties or if it shows similar or worse helium-induced surface degradation compared to pure tungsten, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] .
